The Press

Lives

{{W_LIVES_CAP}} people whose influence genuinely outlasted them, and the one book on each worth your time. {{W_FAMOUS_CAP}} the world remembers; {{N_OBSCURE}} it forgot but shouldn't. Reading lives at volume is the cheapest way to borrow judgment you have not yet earned — a board of directors you will never meet. Every pick carries a note on where specialists would argue with it, because "definitive" is a claim, not a fact. Each is numbered: the founding shelf first, then every life since in the order it joined, and a number never changes.

The Atlas

Founders, coaches, investors, a lion tracker, a surgeon: what each of them taught me, from the notes I take while listening. I chart them as sources and pass no verdict on them.

The method

This is a library, not a credential. It holds what I have read, what I think it means, and — deliberately, in every wing — the places where the people who know most still disagree. A claim without its dispute is half a claim.

The three wings are one method applied to people, three ways round. The Press is the ideas people spent their lives inside; Lives is the people themselves, one book each; The Atlas is the people I listen to now, and the principles I hear more than one of them teach. The library used to run to five wings — a set of field manuals and a trade book of operating lessons. Both were positions stated without anyone standing behind them, and they came down in September 2026 so that everything here is attached to a person you can go and check.

Set in EB Garamond and IBM Plex Mono. Assembled by hand and with AI assistance; figures are checked against a named source, and where I have corrected myself the correction stays visible rather than being quietly patched. The reading wings are set on paper. The Atlas is the only room kept dark: it is drawn as a sea chart, the one room here that is a map rather than a page, and a chart is read by lamplight.

The portraits in Lives are public-domain engravings, paintings and photographs, reduced to the house duotone and set as plates. A life without a safely public image carries the press mark instead of a borrowed picture, which seems the more honest trade. {{W_PLATELESS_CAP}} lives are in that position today. Henrietta Lacks is there by decision; her entry says why at length, and her estate has itself disputed the use of family photographs. Ibn Khaldun, Clair Patterson, Vasily Arkhipov, Emily Warren Roebling, Alice Ball, Edward Thorp and Hedy Lamarr are there because no image of any of them has yet been cleared: no portrait of Ibn Khaldun from his own lifetime is known, Patterson's photographs sit in an archive that grants permission only on request, the one openly licensed photograph of Arkhipov was tagged by an uploader who does not appear to have held the rights to grant it, the Library of Congress portrait of Roebling is a 1953 print of a photograph taken between 1860 and 1880 and the Library records that it found no information on creator or reproduction rights at all, no photograph of Ball has been found under any licence we can stand behind, Thorp is alive and photographed by working photographers, whose pictures are theirs, and the 1939 Los Angeles Times portrait of Lamarr is tagged elsewhere as openly licensed while the library that holds it says, for that collection, that permission to publish must be asked for in writing. The Roebling case is the closest of these: the original is old enough to be out of copyright several times over, and a faithful reproduction of it would add nothing new. It is held back anyway, because “the Library found nothing” is not the same statement as “there are no known restrictions”, and this house has already turned down two images on thinner doubts than that. {{W_CCPLATES_CAP}} plates are licensed rather than public domain, and are credited here because the licence requires it: the Mandela photograph is by South Africa The Good News (sagoodnews.co.za) under CC BY 2.0; the Steve Jobs photograph was taken at WWDC in 2010 by Matthew Yohe under CC BY-SA 3.0; the Tu Youyou photograph was taken in Stockholm on 6 December 2015 by Bengt Nyman under CC BY-SA 4.0; the 1955 photograph of Rosalind Franklin at her microscope is credited to the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology, from the personal collection of her sister Jenifer Glynn, under CC BY-SA 4.0; and the photograph of Samuel Zemurray, taken on 10 January 1934 for the Los Angeles Times, is from the Los Angeles Times Photographic Collection at UCLA Library Special Collections, under CC BY 4.0. Each has been cropped and reduced to the house duotone, which the licences ask us to say. {{W_NARROW_CAP}} more are neither plain public domain nor licensed but held under a narrower claim, and the claim is worth repeating in the holder's own words: the 1939 photograph of Robert Moses is by C. M. Stieglitz for the New York World-Telegram & Sun, held by the Library of Congress, which states that it knows of no copyright restrictions on it; the 1963 photograph of Wu Chien-Shiung at Columbia comes from the Smithsonian Institution Archives, published with no known copyright restrictions; the photograph of Frances Kelsey receiving her award from President Kennedy comes from the National Library of Medicine, which believes the item to be in the public domain; the April 1936 photograph of Frances Perkins is by Harris & Ewing, held by the Library of Congress, which states that it knows of no copyright restrictions on it; the photograph of Edwin Land presenting at Polaroid is by Bernard Gotfryd, held by the Library of Congress, which states that there are no known restrictions on its publication; the 1930s studio portrait of Thomas Midgley Jr. by Blank & Stoller of New York comes from the Science History Institute, which reasonably believes it is not restricted by copyright but says a conclusive determination could not be made; the 1981 photograph of Barbara McClintock holding her Lasker Award and an ear of corn is by Bernard Gotfryd, held by the Library of Congress, which states that there are no known restrictions on its publication; and the photograph of Annie Turnbo Malone is from a Poro College souvenir booklet printed between 1920 and 1927, held by the Smithsonian’s National Museum of African American History and Culture, which lists no known copyright restrictions on it. Everything else came through Wikimedia Commons.

Disclosure

This site was assembled by {{EDITOR}} with substantial help from an AI assistant (Anthropic's Claude) — drafting, checking figures against the named sources, and the build itself. The picks, positions and errors are mine; when an error is found it joins the corrections above instead of disappearing. Lines marked “after” a name are compressed notes of someone's idea, not their words, and nobody named on this site has endorsed it or its readings of them. Portraits are public-domain images, except the {{N_LICENSED}} credited above. The page sets no cookies and runs no analytics. Two things are remembered, only in your own browser and never sent anywhere: the Dusk switch (day or dusk), and how far you got in each entry, so it can mark what you have finished and offer to take you back.
